Section 4 • \(\xi\)3D

4.3 Reduction to \(\mu\) wedges, \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(r)\rvert_{\mu\in(\mu_1,\mu_2)}\)

To combine the transverse and spectral separations into a single 3D separation, both must be expressed in the same units. We can convert \(\Delta\) into a comoving line-of-sight separation, \(r_\parallel\equiv\Delta/\mathcal{J}\), with \(\mathcal{J}\equiv d\Lambda/dr_\parallel\) the local Jacobian of the spectral coordinate; in velocity units \(\mathcal{J}=H(z)/(1+z)\) (Sec. 3.2.4 and Appendix C), evaluated at the effective redshift of the interval. We then define \begin{equation} r\equiv\sqrt{r_\perp^2+r_\parallel^2}, \qquad \mu\equiv\frac{r_\parallel}{r}\in[-1,1], \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad r_\perp=r\sqrt{1-\mu^2}, \qquad \Delta=\mathcal{J}\,r\,\mu, \tag{4.7} \end{equation} where the sign of \(\mu\) keeps the sign of \(\Delta\), relevant for cross-correlations. The per-sample wedge estimator is the average of \(\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\vec{r}_{\perp},\Delta)\) over the portion of the sphere of radius \(r\) with \(\mu\in(\mu_1,\mu_2)\) (Fig. 8, right), with the solid-angle measure \(d\Omega=d\mu\,d\varphi\) (the angular part of \(d^3r=r^2\,dr\,d\mu\,d\varphi\)): \begin{align} \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(r)\Big\rvert_{\mu\in(\mu_1,\mu_2)} &\equiv \frac{1}{2\pi\,(\mu_2-\mu_1)} \int_{\mu_1}^{\mu_2}\! d\mu \int_0^{2\pi}\! d\varphi\; \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{r}_{\perp}\!\left(r\sqrt{1-\mu^2},\varphi\right),\,\mathcal{J}r\mu\right) \notag\\ &= \frac{1}{2\pi\,(\mu_2-\mu_1)} \int_{\mu_1}^{\mu_2}\! d\mu\; \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(r\sqrt{1-\mu^2},\,\mathcal{J}r\mu\right), \tag{4.8} \end{align} where the second line uses Eq. (4.5). The wedge is defined for the radii at which all the lags involved are available, i.e. \(\mathcal{J}r|\mu|<L_\Lambda\) and \(\vec{r}_{\perp}(r\sqrt{1-\mu^2},\varphi)\) within the separations covered by \(\mathcal{A}_\perp\).

In the extreme case \(\mu\in(-1,1)\) the wedge covers the whole sphere and gives the spherical average, \begin{equation} \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(r)\Big\rvert_{\mu\in(-1,1)} = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{-1}^{1}\! d\mu \int_0^{2\pi}\! d\varphi\; \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{r}_{\perp}\!\left(r\sqrt{1-\mu^2},\varphi\right),\,\mathcal{J}r\mu\right) = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int\! d\Omega\;\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{r}\right), \tag{4.9} \end{equation} i.e. the usual isotropic 2PCF \(\xi_{ij}(r)\) (the monopole of its Legendre expansion in \(\mu\)). Narrower wedges are needed only because the statistics are not isotropic in 3D: redshift-space distortions and line shifts make the correlation depend on \(\mu\), and the wedges retain that dependence. For autocorrelations, being even in \(\Delta\) (Eq. (4.6)), the wedges \((\mu_1,\mu_2)\) and \((-\mu_2,-\mu_1)\) coincide, and \(\mu\in(0,1)\) suffices.
